quiz_questions.question: Why is 6-DoF pose tracking from monocular video difficult for reflective or transparent objects?
choices: The object pose has only two rotational degrees of freedom in monocular video.
Appearance cues can be weak or misleading, and many existing approaches require extra inputs such as 3D models, masks, or depth.
The camera intrinsics are never needed when the object surface is reflective.
Transparent objects always produce fully labeled event streams.
quiz_questions.explanation: Textureless, transparent, and reflective surfaces reduce reliable visual evidence. Methods that depend on auxiliary geometry or masks fail when only video is available.

quiz_questions.question: What changes when a rolling-shutter camera is calibrated from ordinary image sequences rather than a target rig?
choices: The method must infer both intrinsics and readout timing from natural motion constraints.
The method can ignore row-wise exposure because bundle adjustment removes it automatically.
The camera becomes equivalent to an event sensor with asynchronous pixels.
The scene must be rendered as Gaussians before any calibration variable can be estimated.
quiz_questions.explanation: Rolling shutter distortion depends on row timing during motion. Self-calibrating bundle adjustment must estimate the readout time ratio along with camera intrinsics.

quiz_questions.question: Why can a geometry-only Gaussian map be reasonable for robotic SLAM?
choices: Navigation and obstacle avoidance depend primarily on spatial geometry, not photorealistic appearance.
Robots cannot use dense maps unless every primitive stores high-frequency color.
Geometry-only maps remove the need for tracking because rendering supplies the pose.
Appearance modeling is always less expensive than storing spatial structure.
quiz_questions.explanation: For downstream robotic tasks, accurate spatial layout can matter more than view synthesis quality. Dropping appearance modeling can focus capacity on geometry needed for motion decisions.

quiz_questions.question: Why split a large-scale Gaussian SLAM system into a feature-based tracking frontend and a structured mapping backend?
choices: The frontend makes photorealistic textures, while the backend guesses camera intrinsics from text.
Lightweight tracking keeps real-time pose updates, while structured sparse mapping controls memory and scene coherence.
The split prevents loop closure because old anchors cannot affect new map regions.
The backend replaces all observations with a fixed batch of unordered images.
quiz_questions.explanation: Large outdoor scenes stress memory and speed. A decoupled design lets tracking remain fast while mapping uses structured anchors and decomposition to scale.

quiz_questions.question: Why are event streams attractive for robotic perception?
choices: They provide low-latency, high-dynamic-range changes at very fine temporal resolution.
They replace all physics simulation with static RGB segmentation masks.
They remove the need for labels because every event is a final action.
They encode only language tokens, avoiding camera calibration entirely.
quiz_questions.explanation: Event cameras report asynchronous brightness changes with microsecond-scale timing and high dynamic range. That makes them useful when fast motion or lighting variation challenges frame cameras.

quiz_questions.question: In unified multimodal pretraining, why study knowledge flow between language, visual understanding, and visual generation?
choices: Because modalities can transfer useful structure, but poor alignment can limit synergy.
Because language always dominates vision once the model has enough parameters.
Because visual generation prevents any need for visual understanding tasks.
Because audio and image patches cannot be used in one architecture.
quiz_questions.explanation: Unified training can let modalities help each other, but the interaction mechanism is not automatic. Measuring transfer and synergy clarifies when integration helps rather than interferes.

questions.question: You are building an XR mapper that must show reconstruction while the user walks. Which fusion choice matches the constraint?
choices: Perform offline 3DGS training after all images are captured.
Use visual-inertial tracking with incremental Gaussian updates for simultaneous tracking and reconstruction.
Disable inertial measurements so the renderer controls all pose estimates.
Batch all context views jointly and prevent causal updates.
questions.explanation: XR needs immediate pose and map updates. Visual-inertial tracking supplies real-time motion estimates while incremental splatting updates the rendered scene.

questions.question: A robotics team lacks labeled event-camera data for a target scene. What is the most direct simulation strategy?
choices: Use a physics-grounded event plugin that generates labeled event streams from a simulated camera.
Train only on still RGB images and infer events from class labels.
Ask the controller to synthesize tactile readings from every event pixel.
Replace event streams with a larger language prompt.
questions.explanation: The stated bottleneck is scarce labeled event data. A simulator with a log-intensity contrast event model can generate high-rate labeled streams for the robot and scene.

gym.taunt: Lose the frame, and every clever sensor becomes a rumor.

questions.question: A mobile robot has accurate short-term tracking but its Gaussian map becomes inconsistent over a campus route. What combination best addresses the issue?
choices: Keep the frontend fast, use structured sparse mapping, and apply long-term coherence constraints as the map grows.
Increase texture resolution in every splat and ignore spatial decomposition.
Switch to event simulation only, since drift is caused by RGB cameras.
Remove loop correction so each segment remains locally independent.
questions.explanation: The failure is long-horizon drift and memory pressure. Robust lightweight tracking plus structured large-scale mapping targets both real-time operation and coherence.

questions.question: Which failure is most likely if a unified multimodal model aligns modalities poorly?
choices: The model gains perfect geometric scale from text alone.
One channel can interfere with another, reducing the intended transfer between language and visual capabilities.
The camera readout ratio becomes exactly known without motion.
Every generated frame becomes a calibrated SLAM keyframe.
questions.explanation: The benefit of unified training depends on useful knowledge transfer. Poor modality alignment can blunt or distort that transfer.

questions.question: Why might a robot SLAM stack prioritize geometry fidelity over novel-view realism?
choices: Control tasks such as navigation and obstacle avoidance use spatial layout more directly than photorealistic color.
Novel-view realism always increases pose accuracy with no compute cost.
Geometry fidelity is irrelevant once a policy has language input.
Obstacle avoidance only requires matching image histograms across frames.
questions.explanation: For control, the map is often used to decide where the robot can move. Accurate geometry supports those decisions even if appearance is simplified.

quiz_questions.question: What problem does training future losses through earlier generated video context address?
choices: Earlier generated latents may be written into keys and values that are not useful for later frames.
The model cannot render any frame unless it has a calibrated camera target.
Motion blur is eliminated by replacing video with unordered image sets.
Rigid-body motion must be ignored so each point can move independently.
quiz_questions.explanation: If historical cache states are frozen, future errors cannot teach earlier generated context how to support later generation. Passing gradients through that history closes the context-supervision gap.

quiz_questions.question: Why model dynamic 4D motion with structured SE(3)-like transformations instead of independent point flows?
choices: Independent point flows always enforce rigid body kinematics automatically.
Real objects often move collectively, so structured transformations encode physical motion more faithfully.
SE(3) transformations remove the need for visual observations.
Structured motion is only useful for static field boundary delineation.
quiz_questions.explanation: Physical objects often undergo coherent rigid-body motion. Treating every point independently can miss the shared geometry of that motion.

quiz_questions.question: Why does egocentric object tracking need memory beyond current detections?
choices: Objects moved by the camera wearer may leave view or become occluded while their locations still matter.
Current detections always include every object touched earlier in the video.
Egocentric cameras provide perfect global maps at each frame.
Object identity is unnecessary once the wearer stops looking at it.
quiz_questions.explanation: The task requires maintaining instance locations online even when objects are out of sight. A track memory carries state across occlusions and viewpoint changes.

quiz_questions.question: Why express visual observations as robot-centric pointmaps for action prediction?
choices: Actions are defined in the robot's 3D frame, so robot-centered geometry reduces camera-view mismatch.
Pointmaps replace language instructions with field-boundary labels.
Camera-frame observations always generalize across all viewpoints without transformation.
Robot-centric geometry prevents any need for large-scale demonstrations.
quiz_questions.explanation: VLA actions live in the robot coordinate frame, while cameras may vary across datasets. Expressing scene geometry robot-centrically aligns perception with the action frame.

quiz_questions.question: Why can overlapping action chunks cause boundary jitter?
choices: Consecutive chunks may predict inconsistent actions for the same time region.
Chunked policies always run slower than single-step policies.
The robot changes its camera intrinsics at each chunk boundary.
Boundary overlap removes all temporal information from the policy.
quiz_questions.explanation: When overlapping regions disagree, execution switches between mismatched proposals. Training and execution must align chunk boundaries rather than only reweighting them later.

quiz_questions.question: What is the advantage of predicting B-spline action parameters instead of discrete-time action chunks?
choices: The policy emits smooth continuous trajectories that can be temporally scaled for faster low-level control.
The policy no longer needs observations because knots encode the whole scene.
The spline forces every manipulation task into the camera frame.
The controller can ignore contact because curves are always collision-free.
quiz_questions.explanation: B-splines parameterize continuous trajectories with knots and control points. Low-level controllers can execute them at higher frequency or adjusted speed without discrete chunk jitter.

side_retention_duels.name: The Memory Rail

questions.question: A mobile manipulator jitters whenever it switches between overlapping action chunks. Which fix targets the cause rather than masking it?
choices: Use seam-aware training and execution so chunk boundaries are learned consistently.
Average the two chunks only at inference and leave training unchanged.
Shorten the camera exposure until the chunk overlap disappears visually.
Move all actions into text tokens and decode them later.
questions.explanation: Inference-time blending can reweight mismatched proposals but does not correct why they disagree. Boundary-aware training changes the predictions themselves.

questions.question: You are converting head-mounted human manipulation videos into robot training data. What transformation is essential?
choices: Retarget actions and render robot-format observations so the data matches robot embodiment.
Keep human hands visible and ask the robot to imitate pixel positions directly.
Discard synchronization because only task labels affect policy learning.
Convert every frame into an unordered SfM collection.
questions.explanation: Human egocentric data differs from robot embodiment and action space. Retargeting and robot-arm visual synthesis make the demonstrations usable for robot policy training.

gym.taunt: Show me a motion plan that survives its next second.

questions.question: A robot must carry an upright object while driving its base and moving both arms. Why might multiple action frames help?
choices: Some parts of the action are simpler in end-effector frames, while transport and whole-body coordination can be simpler in a base-aligned frame.
Multiple frames remove the need for a shared canonical action state.
Every denoiser should optimize an unrelated future trajectory.
A single camera frame is always the easiest coordinate system for contact control.
questions.explanation: Manipulation is multi-frame: local and whole-body components can have different natural coordinates. Synchronized denoising across frames keeps them tied to one canonical trajectory.

questions.question: A generated long video becomes less coherent as early generated context is reused. What training signal is missing?
choices: A loss path that teaches earlier generated history how to become useful context for later frames.
A contact-following reward for every rendered object boundary.
A visual-inertial odometry frontend for all latent tokens.
A field delineation dataset with physical scale labels.
questions.explanation: If future losses cannot update historical cache states, earlier generated latents are not trained for their later conditioning role. Restoring that gradient path targets long-horizon extrapolation.

questions.question: Why combine egocentric memory with robot-centric geometry in a household manipulation system?
choices: Memory keeps track of hidden objects, while robot-centric geometry expresses where actions should happen relative to the robot body.
Egocentric memory replaces coordinate transforms and makes all viewpoints identical.
Robot-centric maps only help after objects leave the field of view.
Both mechanisms mainly improve photorealistic rendering rather than control.
questions.explanation: Hidden-object state and action-frame alignment solve different temporal problems. Together they preserve object continuity and make the retained state actionable.

quiz_questions.question: Why can local sequential glimpses help visual state tracking?
choices: They force the model to update state over observations rather than solve the task from one global image.
They eliminate the need for memory because each glimpse contains the full image.
They make every vision problem independent of sequence length.
They convert camera motion into tactile pressure readings.
quiz_questions.explanation: Sequential glimpses require maintaining and updating state as evidence arrives. That can test length generalization differently from one-shot global image processing.

quiz_questions.question: What does a modular robot program make easier after a manipulation failure?
choices: It exposes intermediate perception and control calls that can be inspected or corrected.
It guarantees zero distribution shift by hiding every internal decision.
It removes the need for perception tools because actions are hard-coded.
It turns all robot actions into photorealistic renderings.
quiz_questions.explanation: Modular programs decompose policy execution into interpretable tool calls. Failures can be localized and edited more directly than in an opaque end-to-end policy.

quiz_questions.question: Why add tactile residual adaptation to a pretrained visual manipulation policy?
choices: Contact success may depend on local force and contact geometry that vision does not capture.
The visual policy cannot move unless every tactile sensor is disabled.
Tactile residuals replace all demonstrations with hand-written geometry rules.
Residual adaptation makes sensor hardware identical across robots.
quiz_questions.explanation: Visual priors can guide motion but miss contact details. A tactile residual can adjust actions using force and contact cues during manipulation.

quiz_questions.question: What problem does generating tactile pressure images from RGB try to reduce?
choices: The scarcity and hardware cost of collecting tactile-equipped training data.
The need for visual observations in all manipulation policies.
The dimensionality of camera poses in bundle adjustment.
The latency of remote GPU scheduling for robot fleets.
quiz_questions.explanation: Tactile datasets are harder to collect and standardize than visual data. Synthesizing tactile signals from RGB can expand supervision for visuo-tactile policies.

quiz_questions.question: Why are explicit contact commands useful for humanoid object interaction?
choices: A body can reach the correct keypoint pose without making the contact needed to affect the object.
Contact commands remove the need for any whole-body controller.
Keypoint tracking already guarantees wiping, sitting, and pushing interactions.
Binary contact labels make visual observations unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explanation: Object interaction often depends on whether the correct body part actually touches the object. Contact commands separate physical interaction from mere pose imitation.

quiz_questions.question: Why can actuator dynamics create sim-to-real error on low-cost servo platforms?
choices: The simple current-to-torque relation can break under friction, hysteresis, backlash, and thermal effects.
Low-cost servos never experience external contact forces.
Actuator models only affect rendering, not trajectory propagation.
Backlash is removed by increasing camera resolution.
quiz_questions.explanation: A simulator that assumes linear torque response can mispredict real motion. Modeling actuator behavior and contact-gated external force perception reduces that mismatch.

side_retention_duels.name: The Contact Bench
side_retention_duels.description: Hands, cameras, and controllers are tested against tasks where pose alone is not enough.

questions.question: A robot wipes a board but often hovers just above the surface while matching the demonstration pose. What signal should be added?
choices: Explicit part-level contact targets with rewards for following them.
A higher-resolution RGB camera with no contact supervision.
A language-only instruction that repeats the wiping verb.
A Gaussian map that removes all tactile feedback.
questions.explanation: The failure is not pose tracking; it is missing physical contact. Contact labels and rewards teach the controller when and where touch must occur.

questions.question: A fleet must call a large robot policy from a remote GPU under tight latency. What system issue must be handled?
choices: Scheduling action chunks across robots with heterogeneous compute and timing demands.
Replacing every robot controller with an offline CAD reconstruction loop.
Ignoring batching because all robots always consume identical action chunks.
Using tactile synthesis to set network bandwidth automatically.
questions.explanation: Serving robot foundation models remotely turns control into a scheduling problem. Simple heuristics can fail when robots have different action consumption patterns.

gym.taunt: If your plan cannot feel the table, it cannot clear it.

questions.question: A contact-rich policy works in videos but fails when grasp force matters. Which combined response is most grounded?
choices: Keep the visual motion prior, add tactile adaptation or tactile prediction, and validate on real contact behavior.
Discard vision entirely because contact makes images useless.
Use keypoint tracking alone since reaching the object proves interaction.
Increase language prompts until force feedback is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Vision supplies scalable priors, but contact geometry and force are separate signals. Tactile adaptation or synthesized touch can provide the missing feedback channel.

questions.question: Why might direct V+L-to-action decoding be preferred for a high-rate VLA controller?
choices: It avoids invoking a large language-model-centered pathway at every control step, reducing compute and memory overhead.
It makes the model independent of visual observations during control.
It guarantees contact stability without tactile or actuator modeling.
It turns all robot commands into globally optimized camera poses.
questions.explanation: An LLM-centered visual-to-language-to-action path can be expensive at each policy call. Directly encoding vision and language for action targets real-time constraints.

questions.question: A dexterous hand learns from one human demonstration. What must retargeting preserve for RL to be useful?
choices: Hand-object motion and contact-relevant references that the robot can physically track.
Only the final object category, because contact modes emerge automatically.
The human camera image exactly, even if robot kinematics differ.
A text summary of the motion with no kinematic reference.
questions.explanation: Retargeting gives RL a physically meaningful reference. For manipulation, preserving hand-object relations matters because contact-rich dynamics are delicate.

quiz_questions.question: Why might a 3D system avoid a latent VAE-style bottleneck when unifying generation and reconstruction?
choices: Latent encoding can lose information about the underlying 3D representation.
Latent encoding always prevents text-conditioned generation.
Pixel-space methods cannot represent geometry at all.
Reconstruction and generation require unrelated coordinate systems.
quiz_questions.explanation: A compressed latent space may discard details needed by both reconstruction and generation. Operating closer to pixel or representation space can reduce that information loss.

quiz_questions.question: What is the benefit of stepwise CAD reconstruction with intermediate geometry checks?
choices: The model can compare the current shape to the target after each operation instead of emitting the entire program blindly.
The model avoids parametric operations and stores only dense video frames.
The model guarantees every mesh becomes a photorealistic Gaussian field.
The model removes the need for editable geometry by rasterizing the final image.
quiz_questions.explanation: Building feature by feature creates opportunities to inspect what remains wrong. That is better aligned with editable CAD than a single opaque program emission.

quiz_questions.question: Why bake high-frequency texture into a compact atlas while keeping lower-frequency geometry features on surfels?
choices: It reduces fragment rendering cost while preserving detailed appearance.
It removes all view dependence from the geometry representation.
It forces every primitive to become a convex triangle.
It makes camera calibration unnecessary for novel views.
quiz_questions.explanation: High-frequency appearance can be expensive during rendering. Baking it into an atlas and pruning weak surfels targets speed while retaining visible texture detail.

quiz_questions.question: Why add deformable boundaries to triangle splats?
choices: Curved and concave structures may require too many primitives when boundaries must stay convex.
Triangle splats cannot lie on a 3D plane unless they become non-convex.
Deformable boundaries replace differentiable rasterization with bundle adjustment.
The control points estimate robot contact forces during rendering.
quiz_questions.explanation: Convex primitive boundaries can inefficiently approximate curved or concave shapes. Learnable boundary displacements add shape flexibility while retaining the base triangle plane.

quiz_questions.question: Why does streaming feed-forward 3DGS need a persistent scene state?
choices: Sequential calibrated views arrive causally, so the system must retain historical 3D information for later updates.
Streaming views are unordered, so no geometry can be reused across chunks.
A persistent state prevents any new Gaussian from being rendered.
Feed-forward reconstruction only works after per-scene offline optimization.
quiz_questions.explanation: Online settings cannot process all context views jointly from the start. A persistent geometry-grounded cache lets each new chunk update an accumulated scene.

quiz_questions.question: Why include automatic success checking, quality filtering, and trajectory smoothing in a scalable demonstration engine?
choices: Large community-collected data are variable, so automated checks convert raw demonstrations into training-ready trajectories.
Filtering is only needed when every task is hand-designed by a central operator.
Trajectory smoothing replaces the need for diverse manipulation tasks.
Success checking prevents robots from collecting browser teleoperation data.
quiz_questions.explanation: Scaling data collection increases heterogeneity and noise. Validation and filtering protect policy training from low-quality or failed demonstrations.

side_retention_duels.name: The Render Conveyor
side_retention_duels.description: A furnace streams views, prunes excess detail, and rejects unstable geometry before it hardens.

questions.question: An online viewer receives calibrated images one chunk at a time. Which design best supports causal updates?
choices: Maintain a voxel-aligned cache of historical 3D tokens and decode new Gaussians after each chunk.
Wait until every possible view has arrived, then run a single fixed-context pass.
Discard historical geometry so each chunk renders independently.
Bake a texture atlas before any camera view is observed.
questions.explanation: Streaming reconstruction needs memory of earlier geometry. A causal cache stores accumulated 3D state while allowing new calibrated views to update the scene.

questions.question: A global farm-boundary mapper fails on cropland textures and topologically complex regions. What capability is most relevant?
choices: Domain-specific scale and topology awareness trained across broad multi-resolution field data.
A generic zero-shot mask model with no geospatial adaptation.
A humanoid contact policy that tracks board-wiping commands.
A rolling-shutter camera model for indoor phone video only.
questions.explanation: Cropland boundaries have domain-specific texture, topology, and scale issues. A wide-area foundation model for field delineation targets those geospatial constraints.

gym.taunt: Render it once and you have a picture; update it forever and you have a world.

questions.question: You need editable mechanical geometry rather than only a realistic rendering. Which representation choice is most appropriate?
choices: A stepwise parametric CAD program checked against target geometry after each operation.
A texture atlas that stores high-frequency color but no editable construction history.
An event-camera stream that records brightness changes at each pixel.
A chunked action policy that smooths robot commands.
questions.explanation: Editable CAD requires explicit operations and intermediate geometry checks. A radiance-only representation may look good but does not provide the same parametric editability.

questions.question: A sparse-camera dynamic capture has missing structures and floating Gaussians. Which intervention matches the failure?
choices: Use complementary depth priors to strengthen geometry supervision under limited views.
Bake high-frequency texture earlier so missing shape becomes invisible.
Increase action chunk length because trajectory continuity creates depth.
Remove all priors so the sparse cameras decide scale alone.
questions.explanation: Sparse cameras weaken geometric constraints. Combining depth cues can supply denser or more reliable structure, reducing missing regions and floating primitives.

questions.question: Why combine streaming reconstruction with automated quality control in a growing 3D or robot-data system?
choices: Incremental state preserves continuity, while validation prevents bad updates or demonstrations from accumulating into the model.
Streaming alone guarantees every new input is geometrically correct.
Quality control matters only for final images, not for training trajectories.
A fixed context batch is always more scalable than causal updates.
questions.explanation: Scaling systems accumulate errors unless incoming data are checked. Persistent state gives continuity, and validation reduces the chance that noisy inputs become lasting structure or training signal.

quiz_questions.question: Why can sliding-window attention reduce KV-cache storage for long contexts?
choices: It bounds attention state to a fixed recent window instead of retaining every prior token's KV entries.
It increases parameter sparsity so fewer model weights are loaded during each decoding step.
It replaces autoregressive decoding with simultaneous denoising across all output positions.
It routes each request to a separate accelerator so cache entries never contend in memory.
quiz_questions.explanation: A fixed window makes stored attention state scale with window size W rather than total context length. The benefit appears only where the model and serving stack respect that windowed dependency.

quiz_questions.question: What changes when long-context RL evaluates the shared prompt without autograd?
choices: The prompt tokens are removed from the context before policy optimization begins.
The target distribution changes because gradients are sampled from a smaller vocabulary.
Activation storage drops because shared prompt computation need not retain full backward-pass state.
All KV-cache entries become reusable across unrelated trajectories without validation.
quiz_questions.explanation: Skipping autograd for shared prompt evaluation avoids storing training activations for that portion. It helps fit million-token RL under a fixed GPU budget while keeping model-specific learning state where needed.

quiz_questions.question: Why can near-memory dequantization improve high-throughput inference?
choices: It changes the trained weights so the model needs fewer attention heads at runtime.
It expands quantized weights as they stream from memory, reducing CUDA-core dequantization overhead and traffic.
It batches unrelated prompts into a single sequence so the scheduler sees fewer requests.
It forces all tokens to use greedy decoding, eliminating sampling variance in the output.
quiz_questions.explanation: Weight-only quantization saves capacity, but GPU-side dequantization can become its own bottleneck. Moving that work into the memory path reduces extra instructions and stalls during large-batch serving.

quiz_questions.question: Why do microsecond-scale collectives matter in long-context decode?
choices: Decode-heavy serving often places many small multi-GPU communications directly on the per-token critical path.
Long contexts eliminate the need for synchronization because all attention is local to one device.
Collective latency matters only during training, since inference never exchanges intermediate tensors.
Small collectives are hidden completely by batching whenever the batch size is greater than one.
quiz_questions.explanation: If every generated token waits on multi-GPU communication, even tiny overheads accumulate into latency and cost. Barrier-free synchronization and hardware-near paths target that critical path.

quiz_questions.question: When can weight-only quantization fail to improve serving throughput?
choices: When the compressed weights require runtime dequantization that adds instruction overhead, traffic, or pipeline stalls.
When the model uses a vocabulary larger than the number of active parameters per token.
When batching is disabled because quantized weights cannot be reused across requests.
When the decoder uses finite automata constraints instead of unconstrained sampling.
quiz_questions.explanation: Quantization reduces model size, but serving speed also depends on how cheaply the compressed values become usable compute operands. A slow dequantization path can offset capacity savings.

quiz_questions.question: Why is bandwidth cost a useful lens for decode-heavy inference economics?
choices: Decode is often bandwidth-bound, so delivered memory bandwidth can determine cost more directly than peak arithmetic throughput.
Bandwidth cost measures benchmark accuracy after quantization better than task-specific evaluation suites.
Memory bandwidth becomes irrelevant when a model activates only part of its parameters per token.
DRAM pricing affects training only, because inference caches are always stored in registers.
quiz_questions.explanation: During decode, moving weights and cache state can dominate token generation. Pricing infrastructure by delivered bandwidth captures a bottleneck that peak FLOPs can hide.

questions.question: A long-context chat service has high prefix reuse across sessions but KV memory keeps growing with conversation length. What change most directly attacks the memory growth?
choices: Introduce SWA-aware prefix cache trees and bounded KV placement for layers that use sliding windows.
Switch every response to beam search so fewer requests are served concurrently.
Increase the GPU clock rate so the same cache occupies less address space.
Disable batching so each request has private cache ownership.
questions.explanation: Prefix trees exploit repeated prompt structure, while SWA-aware placement keeps windowed layers from storing unnecessary full-history state.

questions.question: A cloud model is quantized, but profiling shows dequant kernels blocking throughput at large batch sizes. Which intervention matches the bottleneck?
choices: Move dequantization into the memory subsystem so weights are expanded on the streaming path.
Lengthen the context window so attention compute hides all memory stalls.
Replace all routing logic with random dispatch across accelerators.
Use a stricter JSON schema so fewer tokens are valid at each step.
questions.explanation: The observed bottleneck is not capacity alone; it is the work required to turn compressed weights into usable values. Near-memory dequantization targets that extra path.

gym.taunt: Show me which bytes must live, which may travel, and which can be compressed without breaking the next token.

questions.question: You must serve million-token agents under a fixed GPU budget. Which combination best reduces memory pressure without assuming shorter tasks?
choices: Selective autograd retention for RL, bounded cache where the architecture permits it, and prefix reuse where prompts overlap.
Full attention in every layer, no prefix sharing, and larger batches to amortize all memory growth.
Greedy decoding, random request routing, and higher DRAM clock speeds only.
Finite automata constraints, top-k sampling, and removal of all KV caches.
questions.explanation: The viable path changes storage requirements rather than redefining the task. Each technique reduces retained state only under the dependency structure it can legally exploit.

questions.question: A team buys more GPUs but token latency barely improves because each token waits on memory movement and collectives. What conclusion follows?
choices: The bottleneck is on the byte and communication path, so locality, near-memory work, and lower-latency collectives matter more than raw device count.
The scheduler must remove all batching because batching is always the cause of communication overhead.
The model should be retrained from scratch because decode latency cannot be affected by systems design.
The benchmark is invalid unless it reports only peak FLOPs.
questions.explanation: More compute does not help when the critical path is moving data and synchronizing devices. The abstracts emphasize memory-path and collective-latency optimizations for this regime.

questions.question: A quantized long-context MoE model has good accuracy but unstable throughput across requests. Which risk should be examined first?
choices: Whether active-parameter sparsity, cache growth, dequantization overhead, and prefix hit rates align for the actual request mix.
Whether the model title includes both dense and sparse terminology.
Whether every request can be converted into the same fixed-length prompt.
Whether all answers can be forced into a single JSON grammar.
questions.explanation: Throughput depends on how sparsity, cache behavior, and compressed-weight handling interact with workload structure. Good aggregate quality does not guarantee a stable serving path.

quiz_questions.question: Why can factorized speculative drafts lose acceptance as the speculative budget grows?
choices: Independent future-token marginals fail to model dependencies among candidate tokens, so longer proposals drift from what the target accepts.
The target model stops computing logits after the first accepted token in every speculative block.
The KV cache is deleted after each draft, forcing the verifier to recompute all prompt tokens.
Finite automata constraints make every future token equally likely under the posterior.
quiz_questions.explanation: A longer candidate sequence contains more dependency structure. If the draft treats future positions independently, the proposal increasingly mismatches the target distribution.

quiz_questions.question: Why do diffusion language models need different constrained decoding machinery than autoregressive models?
choices: They use smaller vocabularies, so invalid tokens cannot be represented with a next-token mask.
They sample multiple positions from a factorized distribution during denoising instead of choosing one next token left to right.
They cannot express JSON-like constraints as finite automata.
They always require gradient descent during inference to enforce output format.
quiz_questions.explanation: Autoregressive constraints can mask the next token because generation has a single frontier. Diffusion decoding updates multiple positions, so constraints must condition the whole mean-field posterior.

quiz_questions.question: What makes real-time audio-visual generation different from ordinary offline batching?
choices: It can ignore model-side latency because frames are judged only after the whole clip is generated.
It must preserve signal-to-signal deadlines, so scheduling cannot simply wait for large throughput-friendly batches.
It always uses full attention, making cache management irrelevant to scheduling.
It avoids multimodal encoders, so video resolution has no effect on serving load.
quiz_questions.explanation: Interactive streams have tight end-to-end timing. Larger or delayed batches may improve utilization but break the real-time latency target.

quiz_questions.question: Why does a compiler IR help schedule an autoregressive inference loop on specialized hardware?
choices: It imports the trained model into hardware-aware operator dialects where loop structure and on-chip memory limits can be optimized.
It removes all dependencies between generated tokens, converting decoding into a single matrix multiply.
It guarantees the same schedule is optimal across every accelerator family.
It replaces runtime memory limits with benchmark annotations.
quiz_questions.explanation: An intermediate representation can separate high-level graph structure from target-specific operations. That gives the compiler a place to schedule the loop under hardware memory constraints.

quiz_questions.question: Why can no single speculative drafting structure dominate all real-world workloads?
choices: Different output distributions change the trade-off between draft latency, candidate length, and acceptance probability.
Speculative decoding changes the target distribution, so each domain needs a separate verifier.
All drafting methods become equivalent once the batch size is greater than one.
Autoregressive and diffusion drafts both require identical dependency assumptions.
quiz_questions.explanation: A useful draft must be cheap and likely to be accepted. Workloads differ in predictability and sequence structure, so the best drafting mechanism varies.

quiz_questions.question: What does roughly linear serialization of divergent GPU paths imply for inference kernels?
choices: Branch divergence can reduce effective throughput in proportion to the number of paths even without a super-linear reconvergence penalty.
Independent Thread Scheduling makes all branch-heavy kernels execute at full warp efficiency.
Divergence affects only graphics workloads, not attention or decoding kernels.
Reconvergence overhead grows exponentially with the number of paths on all tested generations.
quiz_questions.explanation: The reported behavior means each divergent path still costs time. Kernel designs with unnecessary branch splits can lose throughput even if there is no extra super-linear penalty.

side_retention_duels.name: The Drafting Yard
side_retention_duels.description: A trial in choosing decoding and scheduling tactics under strict response deadlines.

questions.question: A code assistant has predictable completions for boilerplate but erratic completions for open-ended design prompts. How should speculative decoding be selected?
choices: Use a workload-aware drafting approach, because acceptance and draft efficiency depend on output distribution.
Use the longest possible factorized draft for every request, because longer budgets always increase acceptance.
Disable verification so draft tokens can never be rejected.
Apply finite automata constraints to every prompt, even when no output format is required.
questions.explanation: Predictable regions can support cheaper longer drafts, while open-ended prompts may reject them. The mechanism must adapt to distribution shape.

questions.question: A video conversation model must improve visual legibility without increasing perceived delay. Which constraint should dominate scheduling?
choices: Preserve the signal-to-signal latency budget while allocating extra work to higher-resolution frames.
Maximize batch size first, then display frames whenever the batch completes.
Prefer offline rendering because interactive deadlines are incompatible with multimodal output.
Move all requests to one GPU so inter-device communication disappears.
questions.explanation: The target is richer real-time output at the same latency. Scheduling must protect the stream deadline while absorbing the added resolution cost.

gym.taunt: Spend compute where it shortens the wait, not where it merely looks busy.

questions.question: A service combines JSON-constrained tool calls, free-form reasoning, and short autocomplete. Which inference policy is most defensible?
choices: Use constraint-aware decoding for formatted calls, scaffolded or sampled reasoning where aggregation helps, and speculative drafting where acceptance is high.
Use one universal greedy decoder because all three tasks emit text tokens.
Use diffusion constraints for every task, since finite automata always increase creativity.
Use only parallel traces, because aggregation removes all latency concerns.
questions.explanation: Different tasks expose different dependencies and validity rules. Matching decoding machinery to the constraint and distribution avoids wasted compute.

questions.question: A multi-GPU LLM has high average tokens per second but poor interactive latency. What should be examined before adding larger batches?
choices: Per-token collectives, pipeline placement, draft acceptance, and stream deadlines on the critical path.
Only the total number of parameters, because latency always tracks model size.
Only benchmark accuracy, because latency cannot be improved without lowering quality.
Whether every kernel uses the same branch structure as graphics shaders.
questions.explanation: Average throughput can hide waits that every token must pay. Collectives, scheduling, and draft validation directly affect interactive latency.

questions.question: A factorized draft model is fast but loses benefit on long candidate blocks. What repair best follows from the mechanism?
choices: Introduce dependency-aware proposal structure, such as autoregressive adapters or trees, instead of only increasing block length.
Raise the temperature so rejected candidates become more diverse.
Remove target-model verification so all draft tokens count as accepted.
Shorten the prompt cache because acceptance depends only on memory footprint.
questions.explanation: The failure comes from independent marginal proposals drifting from target dependencies. Adding structure to the proposal can improve acceptance without abandoning speculation.

regions.label: The Serving Exchange
regions.technical_label: The Forked Dispatch · The Scarce Fleet · The Last Petition
regions.summary: Serving is the discipline of sending each request to the right path, allocating scarce devices, and protecting the tail.
regions.learner_goal: Diagnose and apply the mechanisms taught in The Serving Exchange under new constraints.

npc.name: Broker Mina
npc.text: The exchange hears every petition at once. Some need memory, some need deadline, some need locality, and the ruinous ones arrive quietly at the tail of the queue.

prerequisite_links.why: The earlier mechanism supplies the state or invariant needed to reason about the next one.
The earlier mechanism supplies the state or invariant needed to reason about the next one.

quiz_questions.question: Why should a serving layer route speculative decoding by request type?
choices: Because draft cost and acceptance depend on the output distribution, so different requests may favor different proposal mechanisms.
Because routing removes the need for target-model verification in speculative decoding.
Because every request with the same prompt length has the same output distribution.
Because block-parallel diffusion is always lower latency than autoregressive multi-token prediction.
quiz_questions.explanation: Speculation helps only when drafts are cheap enough and accepted often enough. Request type can reveal which distribution the decoder is likely to face.

quiz_questions.question: What routing risk appears in a unified multimodal model family with base, turbo, edit, and edit-turbo variants?
choices: A fast path may meet latency goals but miss the quality or editing capability required by the request.
All variants must share identical throughput, so routing cannot affect service behavior.
Editing requests can be routed to text-only decoding because images are generated after service completion.
Variant choice is irrelevant once bilingual rendering is supported.
quiz_questions.explanation: Different variants imply different speed and capability trade-offs. Routing must respect the requested operation, not just choose the fastest path.

quiz_questions.question: Why can a fixed GPU budget force architectural execution changes for long-context RL?
choices: Because million-token trajectories can exceed feasible activation storage unless shared and model-specific state are retained selectively.
Because RL objectives require every token to be decoded with beam search.
Because GPU count determines reward quality independently of memory use.
Because long-context agents do not need observations once training begins.
quiz_questions.explanation: The budget constraint is memory as much as compute. Long trajectories require execution plans that avoid retaining unnecessary backward-pass state.

quiz_questions.question: Why does memory repricing affect inference fleet allocation?
choices: Decode can be bandwidth-bound, so the cost and availability of DRAM/HBM change which fleets can serve tokens cheaply.
Memory prices affect only offline dataset storage and never accelerator economics.
Higher HBM prices automatically make all open-weight models slower at the same parameter count.
Compute resale removes the need to measure bandwidth delivered.
quiz_questions.explanation: If delivered bandwidth is the limiting resource, its price becomes central to token economics. Fleets purchased under different memory costs can have different cost positions.

quiz_questions.question: Why can local NPU inference improve reliability for operating-system agents?
choices: It reduces dependence on cloud offload, which can introduce reliability and privacy concerns for agentic workflows.
It makes attention independent of data movement across all laptop SoCs.
It guarantees higher throughput than every cloud GPU for long sequences.
It removes the need to map fused attention to accelerator-specific execution.
quiz_questions.explanation: Keeping inference local avoids some network and privacy failure modes. The trade-off is that attention must be mapped efficiently onto diverse NPUs.

quiz_questions.question: Why do small collective delays threaten tail latency in multi-GPU decode?
choices: They can sit on every token's critical path, so rare or repeated microsecond delays accumulate into visible response lag.
They occur only after the final token, so they cannot affect interactive response timing.
They are always hidden by CUDA-core dequantization work.
They disappear whenever the model uses sparse experts.
quiz_questions.explanation: Critical-path communication is paid before token generation can proceed. Repeated small delays can shape the slow end of the latency distribution.

side_retention_duels.name: The Exchange Desk
side_retention_duels.description: A practical trial in dispatching mixed traffic across scarce and unreliable serving paths.

questions.question: A desktop agent must keep working during network instability and handle private screen context. Which serving change best matches the risk?
choices: Move suitable attention kernels onto the local NPU, accepting hardware-specific data-movement work.
Route all requests to the cloud and increase retry count.
Disable agent memory so privacy-sensitive context never enters the model.
Use larger speculative blocks for every local request.
questions.explanation: The risk is dependence on remote service for sensitive interactive work. Local NPU inference addresses that risk but requires careful accelerator mapping.

questions.question: A provider has one low-latency fleet with scarce HBM and one slower overflow fleet. Which request should receive the scarce path first?
choices: Interactive streams and decode-heavy requests with tight per-token deadlines.
Offline batch jobs whose completion time is measured in hours.
Requests with the shortest prompts regardless of output length or deadline.
All image edits, even when users accept delayed completion.
questions.explanation: Scarce low-latency resources should protect requests whose quality depends on timing. Deadline and decode critical path matter more than prompt length alone.

gym.taunt: The mean may flatter you; the last request tells the truth.

questions.question: A platform serves tool calls, image edits, bilingual chat, and long-context agents. What routing policy best handles heterogeneity?
choices: Classify by operation, language/context demands, deadline, and decoder distribution before choosing model variant and execution path.
Route by arrival order only, because FIFO preserves fairness and maximizes quality.
Send every request to the largest model, then recover latency with retries.
Choose the cheapest fleet for every request and measure only aggregate throughput.
questions.explanation: Different traffic stresses different capabilities and bottlenecks. Routing must connect request properties to decoder, model variant, cache, and deadline needs.

questions.question: A service has good p50 latency but bad p99 during long-context multi-GPU requests. Which combined diagnosis is strongest?
choices: Token-critical collectives, cache placement misses, and memory bandwidth contention may be amplifying slow requests.
The model has too many benchmark tasks, so p99 latency is a scoring artifact.
All p99 problems imply the decoder is sampling from an invalid grammar.
Long-context requests cannot be improved without removing all attention layers.
questions.explanation: Tail latency often emerges from stacked waits on the critical path. Multi-GPU communication, cache locality, and bandwidth pressure can hit only certain requests hard.

questions.question: Memory prices rise while demand for real-time multimodal interaction grows. Which trade-off becomes central?
choices: Allocating scarce bandwidth and low-latency devices to requests where delay visibly harms interaction, while sending tolerant work elsewhere.
Increasing resolution for every stream first, because higher quality always improves latency economics.
Using only local NPUs, because they eliminate all memory scarcity.
Disabling routing so each fleet receives an equal number of requests.
questions.explanation: The scarce resource should be spent where timing changes user-visible behavior. Memory economics and real-time deadlines must be handled together.

regions.label: The Systems Gauntlet
regions.technical_label: The Instrumented Mirror · The Double Edge · The Many Roads Trial
regions.summary: Measurement must reveal whether a system keeps quality while changing compute, memory, and workload assumptions.
regions.learner_goal: Diagnose and apply the mechanisms taught in The Systems Gauntlet under new constraints.

npc.name: Auditor Keiko
npc.text: A fast engine can still deceive its master. The gauntlet asks what was measured, under which load, and where the apparent gain stops being true.

prerequisite_links.why: The earlier mechanism supplies the state or invariant needed to reason about the next one.
The earlier mechanism supplies the state or invariant needed to reason about the next one.

quiz_questions.question: Why can a tile-centric simulator be more informative for optimized LLM kernels than a coarse analytical model?
choices: It can represent fine-grained dependency scheduling and compute-memory overlap that coarse models may smooth away.
It ignores memory behavior so arithmetic throughput becomes easier to compare.
It replaces hardware counters with task accuracy scores.
It assumes every kernel has identical tile dependencies across architectures.
quiz_questions.explanation: Optimized kernels often gain speed from how tiles depend on each other and overlap movement with compute. A coarse model can miss those scheduling effects.

quiz_questions.question: What does combining microbenchmarks, counters, and static SASS analysis help determine in warp-divergence testing?
choices: Whether observed timing comes from stable divergence behavior or generation-specific architectural changes.
Whether a model's training data mixture can be recovered from its weights.
Whether JSON-constrained decoding changes the target distribution.
Whether local NPUs outperform cloud GPUs on every workload.
quiz_questions.explanation: Multiple instruments cross-check timing, hardware behavior, and compiled code structure. That makes it easier to distinguish architectural change from measurement artifacts.

quiz_questions.question: Why is activating only part of a sparse model per token an efficiency frontier claim rather than just a size claim?
choices: Because serving cost depends on active computation and cache behavior, while quality must still match relevant dense baselines.
Because inactive parameters are deleted from the released checkpoint during inference.
Because sparse models cannot be evaluated on language or code tasks.
Because cache size always grows linearly even when active parameters are sparse.
quiz_questions.explanation: The useful comparison is capability per active compute and memory behavior, not raw checkpoint size. The abstract ties sparse activation and near-constant cache to benchmark performance.

quiz_questions.question: Why is large-baseline view synthesis a stronger test than nearby-view rendering for single-image 3D generation?
choices: It exposes whether generated primitives are coupled to coherent scene surfaces rather than merely aligned to input pixels.
It removes the need to render a 3D representation at all.
It guarantees that per-scene optimization is cheaper than feed-forward decoding.
It evaluates only texture sharpness, not geometry consistency.
quiz_questions.explanation: Nearby views can look plausible with pixel-aligned primitives. Large viewpoint shifts reveal whether the representation encodes stable 3D structure.

quiz_questions.question: Why can evaluating speculative decoding on one average workload be misleading?
choices: Draft acceptance and latency depend on output distribution, so heterogeneous traffic can reverse which method is best.
Speculative decoding has no verifier, so workload differences cannot affect correctness.
All workloads share the same candidate length once the target model is fixed.
Average workloads always include formal grammar constraints and video deadlines.
quiz_questions.explanation: The speedup depends on how well drafts match likely outputs. A single average can hide domains where a different draft structure wins or fails.

quiz_questions.question: Why is a short-context post-training evaluation insufficient for long-context agents?
choices: Agent observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions can accumulate far beyond the training context regime.
Short contexts cannot compute rewards for any RL algorithm.
Long contexts remove the need for cache management because all tokens are equally recent.
Tool outputs are unrelated to memory pressure during deployment.
quiz_questions.explanation: Deployment trajectories may reach million-token scale while post-training stays much shorter. That gap can hide memory, execution, and generalization failures.

side_retention_duels.name: The Trial Ledger
side_retention_duels.description: A practical trial in choosing measurements that reveal real serving and generation failures.

questions.question: A 3D model looks strong on nearby camera moves but breaks on wide viewpoint changes. What evaluation was missing?
choices: Large-baseline view synthesis that tests whether primitives remain tied to coherent scene surfaces.
A faster single-image encoder benchmark with no rendering step.
A text-only language benchmark to measure prompt following.
A per-scene optimization budget that the feed-forward system never uses.
questions.explanation: Nearby views can mask weak geometry. Large-baseline tests reveal whether the representation survives meaningful camera displacement.

questions.question: A video restyling system changes lighting well but alters mouth motion and gaze. Which quality axis failed?
choices: Identity and performance consistency across facial likeness, expression, eye gaze, and lip synchronization.
Throughput under large-batch language decoding.
Finite-automata validity of generated JSON fields.
Training mixture recovery from released weights.
questions.explanation: The task is not just style transfer; it must keep human performance signals intact. Mouth motion and gaze are part of the stated fidelity target.

gym.taunt: Bring me a measurement that survives contact with the workload.

questions.question: A team claims a new serving stack is better because it improves average throughput on short prompts. What must be tested before trusting deployment?
choices: Long contexts, heterogeneous decoder distributions, tail latency, and quality constraints tied to each request class.
Only whether the model has more parameters than the previous release.
Only the fastest batch size, because deployment can be forced to use it.
Only unconstrained generation, because formatted outputs are a separate product concern.
questions.explanation: Average short-prompt throughput can hide memory growth, routing mismatch, tail delays, and validity failures. Deployment traffic supplies the real constraints.

questions.question: A multimodal model family offers fast and high-quality variants. Which evaluation best maps the frontier?
choices: Measure generation quality, edit control, bilingual rendering, and latency for each variant under the operations it is meant to handle.
Rank every variant by one image aesthetic score and deploy the fastest one.
Evaluate only text understanding because image generation quality is subjective.
Use one latency number from an offline batch to represent all interactive and editing tasks.
questions.explanation: A model family exposes different capability and speed points. The frontier is visible only when each operation is evaluated against its own quality and latency needs.

questions.question: A hardware optimization improves a kernel microbenchmark but not end-to-end serving. Which explanation best integrates the gauntlet?
choices: The benchmark may isolate a real low-level gain while missing routing, cache, communication, or workload effects that dominate the full path.
The microbenchmark must be false because low-level measurements never predict anything.
End-to-end serving ignores kernels, so kernel changes cannot affect latency.
The optimization should be accepted if it improves any one metric, regardless of deployment behavior.
questions.explanation: Focused measurements can be valid yet incomplete. End-to-end behavior depends on how kernel gains interact with scheduling, memory, communication, and request mix.
